title: Viagra May Slow the Spread of Cancer
author: Jake Currie
text: Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisementHealthViagra May Slow the Spread of CancerAnd statins can helpJCBy Jake Currie4:00 PM CDT on August 7, 2026Add Nautilus to GoogleViagra was something of an accident. Developed by Pfizer, sildenafil was a promising drug to relieve chest pain and high blood pressure, but male test subjects noticed certain, uh, side effects. So the drug company went with it, giving it the brand name Viagra and the rest is history. Now sildenafil might have another use preventing the metastasis of cancer cells, according to a new study published in Cancer Research.Subscribe to skip adsFeatured VideoPowered By 10 Amazing Gamma-Ray Burst AnimationShareNextStaySildenafil works by blocking the activity of phosphodiesterase type 5 (PDE5), an enzyme that breaks down cyclic GMP (cGMP), a second messenger involved in a lot of cell functions that also relaxes blood vessel walls. With PDE5 inactive, cGMP accumulates, your blood vessels dilate, and you’re off to the races (so to speak).Researchers led by a team from the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel treated mouse and human cancer cells (cultured from a variety of cancers) with sildenafil and monitored what happened. They discovered cGMP has a side hustle, just like sildenafil. It binds to a protein that transports cholesterol in cells, which can be used to build cell membranes. These membranes come in handy for cancer cells when they’re striking out to seek their fortune in other parts of the body, and they’re particularly vulnerable to supply disruption from elevated cGMP activity, the researchers found.  Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisement
